doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: Is the music simple or complex?
summary: Fleck says the music is simple compared with classical, Indian or other jazz. They seek odd meters that feel natural, and he sees the band's uniqueness in its mixture of influences.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You had made a statement in an interview I saw about you felt your music was simple on a symbolic level. Can you expand on that? I think it’s a really interesting statement.

Well I think they were asking about that a lot of the material you write and perform is pretty complex from chord structures and melodies, and then when you guys start improvising it can get very complex. Yet you still felt that there was a simplicity about it that people who might not understand it technically can still like –

Right. All right. Well it just depends what you’re comparing it to. Because I mean if you’re listening to great classical music or if you’re listening to different kinds of jazz through different periods or Indian music, our music would be just pretty simple. You know what I mean? So it depends on the context of what you’re comparing it to. I mean if you’re used to listening to jam bands, or just straight ahead bebop just in four-four that’s complex in the soloing, but the rest of it, the structures can be, I don’t think any of them are very complex. I really don’t. I think we’re always looking for a simple, like if we’re looking for a seven, if we’re going to play in seven, we’re looking for a seven that

feels like it’s in four. If we’re looking for an eleven, we want it to feel like it’s in four. We want to find a way to make what seem to be more complex forms feel very natural and comfortable. But that’s something people have been doing for a long time too. So I’m very aware of the overall context of music, the centuries of music or as much of it as I’ve been exposed to and what’s actually new about our group is probably just a combination of things that haven’t come together before. But in terms of reinventing music, no. We’re not on that level. I think there’s people that are, but no, what I think is unique about us is the combination of influences that have come together into a different, very personal mixture that’s expresses who we are as people. And so that, I love that about our band. That to me is our achievement, is that we’ve been able to keep it together and keep developing as musicians. Everybody’s still getting better as players and we’re getting better at playing as a group. And those are the things that I’m most proud of. But I mean I play some Bach, and I know what that is, and I’ve never written anything on a level of that complexity or depth. I don’t see myself in that way. But I think what we’re doing is personal. And I’m proud of that.
